case_studies.title: BinXSight: Fast Binary Program Summarization via Hierarchical Modular Decomposition
case_studies.abstract: Binary code summarization (BCS) is crucial in fields such as cybersecurity. Particularly, program-level BCS can quickly provide a comprehensive overview of an entire stripped binary without in-depth manual reverse engineering. However, a binary often contains numerous functions with complex interactions, making it challenging to extract its functionality efficiently. Moreover, existing methods focus solely on function-level without considering contextual information, limiting their applicability to program-level analysis. Towards comprehensive and fast program-level BCS, we propose BinXSight, an LLM-powered framework based on hierarchical modular decomposition. Specifically, we first propose binary graph, a new data structure composed of four graphs, to comprehensively represent a binary. Then, based on the binary graph, we hierarchically decompose functions into modules and select the most significant ones. Finally, BinXSight generates a program-level summary from these module summaries. We evaluate BinXSight on stripped binaries across various sizes, fields, platforms, and architectures. Results show that BinXSight outperforms baselines by 23.18% to 46.99%, and summarizes a binary with about 3K functions in 24.3 seconds on average. In addition, a user study with 27 experts shows that BinXSight's high-quality summaries help users quickly understand the whole binary. Our case analysis on recent real-world malware further demonstrates its practical utility.
case_studies.summary: BinXSight quickly turns a stripped binary with thousands of functions into a concise, readable summary in just under 30 seconds. It uses a new graph structure to capture all function interactions, then splits them into key modules and stitches those into a program‑level overview. The result is a 23‑47 % speed and accuracy gain over existing tools, enabling experts to spot malware behaviour almost instantly.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, use BinXSight to scan deployed binaries for hidden malware: 1) run BinXSight on each binary in your image registry, 2) review the generated summary for suspicious modules, 3) flag any binaries with anomalous behaviour for quarantine or further analysis.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical tool for program-level binary summarization, directly aiding security analysts and reverse engineers who work with infrastructure-related binaries. The approach uses LLMs and a novel graph representation, indicating a move toward deployable AI, though the abstract suggests a prototype rather than a production-ready system, hence a moderate maturity score. The methodology could be packaged as a commercial or internal tool for malware analysis and threat intelligence, giving it solid monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: Isonomy: Isolating Every Request from Timing Side Channels at Nearly Full-Sharing Throughput in Multi-Instance LLM Prefill
case_studies.abstract: Many long prompts share a prefix, and reusing its cached keys and values saves prefill computation. A cache hit, however, makes the first token arrive earlier and can reveal that another request used the same prefix, so providers share the cache only within an account. Under least privilege, even permission to send and pay for requests should not expose other requests' prompts in the same account. This matters because agents send unreviewed requests carrying private data, resellers pool users behind one account, and creden-tials can be stolen. Isonomy therefore isolates each request by default and lets requests opt into explicit sharing groups. Rather than give up reuse, it keeps one cache shared across accounts and hides only hits on prefixes cached outside a request's group. We target deployments where clients cannot observe one another's load, because there it suffices to hide these hits in the request's own timing. On three commercial APIs, our listeners could not distinguish added prefill work from a short request beyond measurement noise. Built on vLLM, Isonomy's gateway applies the deployment's routing rule to load and visible cache entries only, which yields the instance where the request would run if hidden hits missed. On that instance, the prediction mode estimates when the first token would be ready from the queue and the visible prefix, and gates its release. The execution mode instead reserves the work a hidden hit skips and fills it with other requests' prompts where possible. In direct-probe tests on two, four, and eight instances with every request isolated, both modes kept the upper bound on a probe's advantage within measure-ment noise at both prefix lengths. At saturation, the prediction mode retains 0.98 of unprotected sharing's throughput on two workloads with account labels, whereas isolation by account retains 0.95, or 0.80 where more reuse crosses accounts.
case_studies.summary: Isonomy blocks timing side‑channel leaks in LLM prefill caches by isolating each request while still allowing efficient key/value reuse across accounts. It builds a gateway on vLLM that masks cache‑hit timing, achieving near‑full throughput (up to 98% of unprotected sharing). The result is safer multi‑tenant LLM services without major performance loss.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage shared LLM deployments, enable Isonomy’s request‑isolation gateway: 1) integrate the Isonomy plugin into your vLLM stack; 2) configure explicit sharing groups per tenant; 3) verify that throughput stays above 95% on your workloads. If you already use account‑level cache isolation, add Isonomy to avoid timing leaks from shared cache hits.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical mechanism to mitigate timing side‑channels in multi‑instance LLM deployments, directly affecting how IT engineers configure and secure LLM APIs, particularly in shared‑account scenarios. The solution is built on top of vLLM and includes empirical tests on commercial APIs, indicating a working system rather than a purely theoretical proposal. While not immediately available as a commercial product, the approach can be adopted or sold as a deployment service within a few weeks, especially in environments already using vLLM or similar serving stacks. Hence moderate impact, medium maturity, and actionable monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: Decision Models for Multilingual Emotion Classification: A Comparative Study Against LLMs and Encoders
case_studies.abstract: Decision models receive a question with a closed list of answers and return a probability for each answer instead of free text. They promise low latency and robustness to prompt wording, but no study has compared several of them with fine-tuned encoders across languages. We ask whether systems used without training on labelled data (zero-shot) can replace fine-tuning, and what the decision format adds over a general-purpose large language model (LLM). We compare three decision models (Jev, OpenAI Decisions, Strands Decider 2B) and two LLMs (GPT-6 Luna, Qwen3.5-2B), given Italian instructions, with two fine-tuned multilingual encoders (tabularisai, XLM-EMO) on four emotions (joy, sadness, anger, fear) in 10 social-media datasets in five languages, with paired difference and equivalence tests. The three best zero-shot systems (two decision models and one LLM) score on average about one macro-F1 point below an encoder fine-tuned on the target dataset; our test sets cannot exclude a gap of 4-5 points, and on single datasets either approach wins by up to 22 points. They beat encoders fine-tuned on another dataset by 8-15 points, though against XLM-EMO this may not extend to new datasets, and instructions in each text's language change their results by under 1 point. Exploratorily, they beat the strongest public emotion model used as is by about 6 points. OpenAI's decision endpoint matches GPT-6 Luna, the LLM it runs on, at a fifth of its median latency, and a 2-billion-parameter decision model beats a same-size general LLM by 10 points, owing to its training, not the decision format. The best zero-shot systems, the LLM included, have an SD of about 1 point across prompts. Without labelled data they are a strong default, and decision models add lower latency and, unlike generative LLM use, per-option probabilities. Fine-tuning won by a wide margin only on the largest dataset, GoEmotions.
case_studies.summary: Decision models can classify emotions in multiple languages with only one macro‑F1 point lower than a fine‑tuned encoder, and they are faster and give per‑option probabilities. They were tested against two fine‑tuned multilingual encoders and two LLMs on 10 social‑media datasets across five languages. The best zero‑shot systems matched a large LLM’s accuracy but ran five times faster and without any training data.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, consider deploying a decision model endpoint (e.g., OpenAI Decisions) for emotion analysis: step 1, choose a small model that gives per‑option probabilities; step 2, host it in a low‑latency container; step 3, monitor accuracy against your own labelled data to verify the ~1 macro‑F1 gap.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents comparative studies of decision models and LLMs for emotion classification, focusing on research methodology and performance metrics across languages. It offers limited direct applicability to IT engineers managing cloud, SaaS, or security infrastructure. While the discussed APIs could be invoked, the study does not provide actionable integration guidance, tooling, or deployment-ready solutions for typical IT workloads. The maturity level is moderate because the models are available via API, but the research nature and lack of implementation details reduce immediate usability. Monetisation potential is low as the work does not present a clear product or service that can be sold or deployed within 90 days. Overall, the impact on everyday IT infrastructure operations is marginal, leading to a low total score.

case_studies.title: Decision Columns as an Index: Interpretable Embeddings for Explainable Entity Matching and Search
case_studies.abstract: Business data systems must determine whether records refer to the same entity and retrieve records satisfying requests whose decisive properties are implicit. As agents act on these records, both tasks require auditable reasons. Dense embeddings perform well but offer opaque coordinates, cannot be filtered by meaning, and require corpus re-encoding to add new properties. We propose interpretable embeddings built from decision columns: each column stores a decision model's calibrated answer to a natural-language question, with outcomes yes, no, or not stated. A record's embedding is its answers across an ordered set of questions. Similarity decomposes exactly into per-question contributions, and new questions add coordinates without altering existing ones. On public product benchmarks, question-space retrieval matches dense candidate generation statistically in a retrieve-then-verify entity matcher, while providing exact explanations for accepted matches. Questions derived from retrieval failures triple mean reciprocal rank without re-encoding prior answers. For search, inferring the attributes of a suitable result outperforms encoding only the literal request, and combining question-space and dense scores improves retrieval, though not at our prespecified confidence threshold. A single small neural network predicts the full interpretable vector from an existing dense embedding, enabling corpus backfilling from a few thousand labeled rows at roughly 1/200 the cost. We position interpretable embeddings as a complementary, readable retrieval channel for explaining matches, filtering on attributes, and extending indexes as failures expose missing facts.
case_studies.summary: This research tackles the lack of interpretability in dense embeddings used for entity matching and search. The authors created decision‑column embeddings where each dimension is a calibrated yes/no/unknown answer to a natural‑language question, enabling per‑question explanation of similarity. Results show comparable retrieval performance to dense embeddings while providing clear explanations and easy index extension.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1) Identify key attributes that need auditability in your data matching workflows. 2) Map those attributes to natural‑language questions and generate decision columns using a lightweight model. 3) Store the resulting vectors in your index; you can add new questions without re‑encoding the whole corpus, and you gain transparent explanations for matches.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a novel embedding approach for entity matching and search that offers interpretability. However, it is primarily a research prototype with no evidence of deployment in real IT infrastructure, limited applicability to existing SaaS or cloud environments, and no clear pathway for immediate monetisation or integration by UK IT engineers. The concepts may inspire future tools, but practical impact today is minimal.

case_studies.title: DistDNA: Language Model Fingerprinting under Stochastic Decoding
case_studies.abstract: Behavioral fingerprints identify a large language model (LLM) from its responses to a shared set of prompts, enabling applications such as verifying whether a deployed model corresponds to the checkpoint it claims to be. Deployed models, however, are commonly served with stochastic decoding, under which the same model may produce different responses to an identical prompt, depending on an unknown temperature and top-$p$ setting. Existing representations such as LLM DNA provide limited treatment of this variation. A natural remedy is to characterize models by their response distributions, which, however, raises two challenges. First, each distribution must be estimated from only a small number of sampled responses. Second, a change in decoding setting can alter responses to the same extent as a change of checkpoint. Consequently, fingerprint distances alone provide an incomplete basis for model identity, and identification typically relies on a classifier trained jointly on fingerprints from many checkpoints. We propose DistDNA, which represents a model by its prompt-conditional response distributions and compares models by promptwise maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). The model under examination is assigned to the known checkpoint whose reference fingerprints, collected at several decoding settings, lie nearest to its own, without training a classifier. We show that finite sampling adds variance-dependent terms to the expected squared fingerprint distance, with these terms decreasing as $O(1/R)$ for equal response counts, where $R$ is the number of responses per prompt. Experiments across 115 model checkpoint entries demonstrate that DistDNA improves identification accuracy over the strongest baseline, LLM DNA, by 10.36%.
case_studies.summary: DistDNA lets you recognise which exact LLM checkpoint you’re talking to, even when the model uses random decoding. It builds a fingerprint of each prompt’s response distribution and matches your instance to the closest known checkpoint using maximum mean discrepancy. The result is a 10‑point jump in identification accuracy over previous methods.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM deployments, first collect a few responses from each prompt at a few temperature/top‑p settings, store these as fingerprints, then use DistDNA’s MMD routine to match new outputs to the right checkpoint and detect if your model has been swapped or mis‑labelled.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a method for fingerprinting LLMs under stochastic decoding, which could help verify deployed models. However, its direct relevance to everyday IT infrastructure tasks is limited. The approach is experimentally validated but not released as a usable tool or service, and there is no clear path for rapid monetisation by an IT engineer.
